title: Reference Types
description: Learn about C# reference types — classes, strings, arrays, and collections — including heap allocation, null references, and shared state.

data.text: While value types store data directly, **reference types** store a reference (essentially a memory address) that points to the actual data on the **heap**. When you assign a reference type variable to another, you copy the reference — not the object itself. Both variables now point to the same piece of data on the heap.

This behavior is called **reference semantics** and it's one of the most important concepts in C#. When you pass a reference type to a method or assign it to another variable, changes made through one reference are visible through all other references to the same object.

data.caption: Reference types live on the heap. Variables hold a reference (pointer) to the heap object, not the data itself.

data.title: Built-in reference types in C#:
items: **array** — fixed-size, zero-based collection of elements of the same type
**class** — the primary way to define custom reference types
**interface** — defines a contract that classes implement
**delegate** — type-safe function pointer for callbacks and events
**List<T>, Dictionary<K,V>** — generic collection types from System.Collections.Generic

data.text: Strings in C# are reference types, but they behave unusually in one important way: they are **immutable**. Once a string is created, its content can never change. Any operation that appears to modify a string (like `ToUpper()` or `Replace()`) actually returns a brand new string object, leaving the original untouched.

data.title: String Immutability
data.text: Because strings are immutable, repeated concatenation in a loop (e.g., `s += x`) creates many temporary strings and is very slow. Use `StringBuilder` for efficient string building in loops.

data.title: Using StringBuilder for Efficiency

data.text: An **array** is a fixed-size, zero-indexed collection of elements of the same type. Arrays are reference types — the array variable holds a reference to the array object on the heap. The array's length is fixed at creation and cannot be changed.

data.title: Working with Arrays

data.text: Arrays have a fixed size, which is often inconvenient. The `List<T>` class provides a resizable array-like collection that can grow or shrink dynamically. It is the most commonly used collection in C#. Other useful collections include `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` for key-value pairs and `Queue<T>` / `Stack<T>` for first-in-first-out and last-in-first-out patterns.

cards.title: Value Types
cards.description: Store data directly. Copied on assignment. Typically on the stack.
pros: Independent copies prevent accidental shared state
cons: Copied fully — expensive for large data

cards.title: Reference Types
cards.description: Store a reference to heap data. Shared on assignment. Garbage collected.
pros: Efficient for large objects (only the reference is copied)
cons: Allocation on the heap is slower
Shared state can cause bugs if not managed carefully

data.title: NullReferenceException
data.text: The most common runtime error in C#. It occurs when you try to access a member (method, property, field) on a reference type variable that is `null`. Always check for null before accessing members, or use the null-conditional operator (`?.`) introduced in C# 6.

Exercise: Build a Task Manager
data.description: Create a simple task manager using List<string> and demonstrate reference semantics.
steps: Create a `List<string>` called `tasks` and add at least 3 tasks
Print the count and each task
Demonstrate reference semantics: assign `tasks` to a second list called `shared` and add a new item to `shared`. Print `tasks` to show the change is visible through both references.
Create a `List<string>` called `independentTasks` and use `.ToList()` to create a true copy. Add to `independentTasks` and verify `tasks` is unchanged
data.expectedOutcome: A console program showing shared state via reference assignment and independent copies via `.ToList()`. Understanding why `shared` and `tasks` see the same changes.

items.question: Is string a reference type even though it seems to act like a value?
items.answer: Yes. `string` is a reference type — the variable holds a reference to the string data on the heap. However, strings are immutable, which makes them behave more like value types in practice (e.g., equality compares content, not reference).

items.question: What is the difference between `=` for value types and reference types?
items.answer: For value types, `=` copies the entire value. For reference types, `=` copies only the reference (the memory address). Both variables then point to the same heap object.

items.question: When is an object eligible for garbage collection?
items.answer: When no reachable references point to it. The .NET garbage collector periodically reclaims heap memory for objects that are no longer accessible from any live variable or object graph.

items.question: Why is string immutable?
items.answer: Immutability enables string interning (saving memory by sharing identical strings), thread safety, and security (e.g., file paths can't be modified after validation). The trade-off is that any modification creates a new string.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Reference types store a pointer to heap data
Assignment copies the reference, not the object
Changes through one reference are visible through all references
string is a reference type but immutable
Use List<T> for dynamic collections instead of fixed arrays
Always check for null to avoid NullReferenceException
data.takeaway: Reference types enable complex data structures and polymorphism. Understanding when data is shared vs copied is essential for writing correct C# code.
